items.stimulus:
Four people give their views on lowering the voting age from 18 to 16.

Speaker 1 (a secondary-school teacher): Sixteen-year-olds already study civics at school, so they know how parliament works and how to fill in a ballot paper. Letting them vote while that lesson is fresh would turn classroom knowledge into a habit. People who vote in the first election for which they are eligible tend to keep voting, so starting at sixteen, when most still live at home and attend school, would raise turnout over a lifetime.

Speaker 2 (a youth worker): The question is not whether teenagers are clever enough to vote; plenty of adults vote with little information. The question is fairness. Sixteen-year-olds can take paid jobs and pay income tax on their wages. If the state takes a share of their earnings, they should have a say in how that money is spent.

Speaker 3 (a psychologist): Research on decision-making separates 'cold' choices, made slowly with time to reflect, from 'hot' choices, made quickly under emotion or peer pressure. Teenagers perform close to adult levels on cold tasks but worse on hot ones. Voting is a cold task: a campaign lasts weeks and the ballot is cast alone. On this evidence, sixteen-year-olds are capable voters.

Speaker 4 (a retired judge): The age of adulthood has to be set somewhere, and it should be consistent. At sixteen, a person cannot sign a binding contract, serve on a jury or buy alcohol. Granting the vote while withholding these other adult rights sends a confused message. If sixteen-year-olds are mature enough to choose a government, they are mature enough for the rest; if not, they should wait until eighteen.
items.question: Speaker 2 and Speaker 4 would most likely agree that

options.text: sixteen-year-olds are mature enough to make sound political choices.
the voting age should be lowered to sixteen.
the voting age should be considered alongside the other legal rights and duties of sixteen-year-olds.
a person's intelligence or level of political knowledge has no bearing on whether they should be allowed to vote.

items.stimulus:
Critics of zoos often picture a lonely bear pacing a concrete pit. That image belongs to the past. The best modern zoos are not entertainment venues with conservation added as an afterthought; they are conservation institutions that happen to welcome visitors, and they deserve to be judged as such.

Consider breeding. When a species collapses in the wild, a managed population in captivity can act as an insurance policy. Several species of frog, bird and antelope that disappeared from their native ranges survived only because zoos kept breeding groups, and some have since been returned to restored habitat. Coordinated breeding programmes, in which zoos in many countries share a single record of every animal's ancestry, allow keepers to pair animals so that genetic diversity is preserved over generations. No single institution could manage this alone.

Zoos also fund field work. Part of every ticket sold supports rangers, habitat surveys and community projects far from the zoo itself. Visitors who will never travel to a rainforest help to protect one simply by spending an afternoon watching gibbons.

Then there is education. People protect what they care about, and they care about what they have seen. A child who has watched a rhinoceros wallow in mud is more likely, as an adult, to support laws protecting rhinoceroses than one who has only seen a photograph.

Opponents reply that wild animals suffer in captivity. Some do, and a zoo that cannot meet an animal's needs should not keep it. But the wider public has plainly reached its own verdict. Visitor numbers at well-run zoos have risen steadily for two decades, which shows that people have recognised that zoos are good for the animals in them.

Abolishing zoos would not return a single animal to a safe forest. It would simply remove one of the few institutions that combines scientific breeding, funding for the wild and public engagement. The right response to bad zoos is to make them better, not to close the good ones.

items.stimulus:
When an infectious disease spreads quickly, health authorities want to know who has been near whom. Smartphone contact-tracing apps promise to supply this information faster than any team of human interviewers. They also raise an obvious worry: a device that records your contacts can reveal where you go, whom you meet and when.

The debate is usually framed as a trade-off. On one side sits public health, which seems to demand as much data as possible; on the other sits privacy, which seems to demand as little. Framed this way, each gain for one value is a loss for the other, and the only question is where to draw the line.

This framing is misleading. A contact-tracing app works only if a large share of the population installs it and keeps it running. Where installation is voluntary, the app's usefulness therefore depends on whether people trust it. An app that sends location histories to a central server may collect richer data from each user, but if many people refuse to install it, it will trace fewer contacts than a more modest app that most people accept. Beyond some point, collecting more data produces less public health benefit, not more.

It does not follow that privacy should always win. If a disease were deadly enough, a government might justifiably require participation, and in that case trust would matter less to the app's reach. Nor does every privacy protection improve uptake; some people would refuse any app, however carefully designed.

What follows is narrower. Where participation is voluntary, designers who want to protect public health have a practical reason, not only a moral one, to limit what their apps collect. Strong safeguards, such as storing data on the phone rather than on a server, deleting it after a few weeks and recording proximity rather than location, are not concessions extracted from public health. They are part of what makes the public health tool work.

items.stimulus: A ferry runs between two jetties, Kell and Marro, which are 24 km apart on a river. Marro is downstream of Kell. The ferry's speed in still water is 10 km/h, and on a normal day the river current flows at 2 km/h. Travelling downstream, the ferry's speed over the ground is its still-water speed plus the current; travelling upstream, it is its still-water speed minus the current. Ignore time spent at the jetties.
items.question: On a day when the current is faster than normal, the ferry's round trip from Kell to Marro and back takes 6 hours 24 minutes. Its still-water speed is still 10 km/h. What is the speed of the current on that day?

options.text: 3 km/h
4 km/h
5 km/h
6 km/h

items.explanation_ko: 1) 유속을 c라 하면 24/(10 + c) + 24/(10 − c) = 6.4시간(6시간 24분 = 6.4시간). 2) 선택지를 대입: c = 5이면 24/15 + 24/5 = 1.6 + 4.8 = 6.4시간으로 일치. 3) 참고로 c = 4이면 24/14 + 24/6 ≈ 1.71 + 4 = 5.71시간, c = 6이면 24/16 + 24/4 = 1.5 + 6 = 7.5시간. 오답: A 3 km/h는 약 5.3시간으로 너무 짧다. B 4 km/h는 약 5.7시간. D 6 km/h는 7.5시간으로 너무 길다. 어림 요령: 24분 = 0.4시간으로 바꾼 뒤 나누어떨어지는 선택지부터 대입한다. 유형 팁: 분수 방정식 문장제는 선택지 대입이 가장 빠르다. → 정답 C

items.stimulus:
Paper was first made in China, where by the early centuries CE craftworkers were pounding plant fibres such as hemp and mulberry bark into a pulp, spreading it thinly on a screen and leaving it to dry. For several hundred years, the technique remained largely within China and neighbouring regions.

A well-known story dates paper-making's westward journey to 751 CE, when, after a battle near the Talas River in Central Asia, Chinese prisoners supposedly taught the craft to their captors in Samarkand. Historians now treat this account with caution. Fragments of paper found along the trade routes show that paper itself was travelling west well before 751, and the story appears in sources written long after the event. What is clearer is that within a few decades of the battle, paper was being produced in Samarkand and then in Baghdad, where the administration of a large empire created heavy demand for a writing material cheaper than parchment and less fragile than papyrus.

The craft did not simply move; it changed as it moved. Mulberry trees were scarce in much of western Asia, so papermakers turned to linen rags, which were plentiful in cities. Centuries later, workshops in Europe made further changes, using water-powered hammers to beat the rags into pulp and attaching wire designs to their moulds to leave a watermark identifying the maker.

The spread of paper-making is sometimes told as the story of a secret escaping, as though knowledge passed intact from one people to another at a single moment. The evidence suggests something more gradual: a technique carried by traders, officials and artisans, and reshaped at every stop by local materials and local needs.
items.question: Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage about the story of the Talas River prisoners?

options.text: It was entirely invented by later writers.
It was first recorded by people who saw the battle near the Talas River.
It cannot explain how paper came to be present in regions west of China before 751 CE.
It explains why papermakers in Baghdad and Samarkand used linen rags instead of mulberry bark.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 글에 따르면 무역로에서 발견된 종이 조각은 751년보다 훨씬 전에 종이가 서쪽으로 이동했음을 보여 준다. 2) 751년 사건이 그 이전의 종이 존재를 설명할 수는 없다. 오답: A 역사가들은 '신중하게' 다룰 뿐 완전히 지어낸 이야기라고 단정하지 않는다. B 오히려 사건보다 훨씬 뒤에 쓰인 기록에 나온다고 했다. D 아마포 사용은 뽕나무 부족으로 설명된다. 유형 팁: 추론은 본문 근거 두 개(연대, 종이 조각)를 연결해 나오는 결론을 고르고 단정적인 선택지는 경계한다. → 정답 C

The methods and materials of paper-making changed as the craft spread to new regions.

items.question: Which one of the following situations most closely matches the writer's account of how paper-making spread?

A cooking method passes from country to country and is altered at each stage to use the ingredients available locally.
The same tool is invented independently, at about the same time, by two communities that have no contact with each other.
A technology is banned by a government and forgotten until it is rediscovered centuries later.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 글쓴이의 설명: 기술이 상인·관리·장인을 통해 점진적으로 전해지며 각 지역의 재료와 필요에 맞게 바뀌었다. 2) B는 전파와 현지 재료에 따른 변형이라는 두 요소를 모두 갖추었다. 오답: A 비밀이 한순간에 그대로 유출되는 이야기로, 글쓴이가 부정한 모델이다. C 독립 발명은 전파가 아니다. D 단절과 재발견은 점진적 전파와 다르다. 유형 팁: 적용 문제는 본문 모델의 핵심 요소를 2개 이상 뽑아 모두 맞는 상황을 고른다. → 정답 B

items.question: A small farm keeps only chickens and goats. The farmer counts 30 animals in total and 84 legs altogether. How many goats are on the farm?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 30마리가 모두 닭이라면 다리는 60개. 2) 실제는 84개로 24개가 더 많고, 닭 한 마리를 염소로 바꿀 때마다 다리가 2개 늘어난다. 3) 24 ÷ 2 = 12마리가 염소. 확인: 12 × 4 + 18 × 2 = 48 + 36 = 84. 오답: A 닭의 수(18). C 다리 수를 4로 나눈 값(84 ÷ 4). D 동물 수를 반으로 나눈 값. 어림 요령: '모두 닭' 가정 후 차이를 2로 나눈다. 유형 팁: 두 종류 합계 문제는 한쪽으로 다 가정하고 차이로 구한다. → 정답 B

items.stimulus: At Brightwell Logistics, about 30% of warehouse staff leave each year. In exit interviews, the reason departing staff gave most often was pay. The operations manager therefore plans to raise warehouse wages by 10%, which would bring them level with the best-paying warehouse in the district. The increase would cost the company about as much as it currently spends each year on recruiting and training replacement staff. She expects the rise to reduce staff turnover substantially within a year.
items.question: The manager's expectation depends on which one of the following assumptions?

options.text: No other warehouse in the district will raise its wages over the next year.
Pay is the only reason that warehouse staff leave Brightwell.
Staff who have stayed at Brightwell are satisfied with their current pay and would not leave for a higher wage elsewhere.
Many departing staff who named pay as their reason were giving their real reason, not just the easiest one to state.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 관리자는 퇴사 면담에서 가장 많이 나온 이유(급여)를 근거로 임금 인상이 이직을 줄일 것이라 기대한다. 2) 이 추론은 면담 답변이 실제 퇴사 이유를 반영한다는 전제가 있어야 한다. 3) 부정하면(급여는 말하기 쉬운 핑계였을 뿐) 인상해도 이직이 줄지 않으므로 논증이 무너진다. 오답: A '어떤 경쟁사도 인상하지 않는다'는 지나치게 강하다. 조금 인상해도 계획은 여전히 효과가 있을 수 있다. B 급여가 '유일한' 이유일 필요는 없다. 주요 이유이기만 하면 된다. C 남은 직원의 만족 여부나 이직 의향은 떠난 직원 분석과 무관하며 가정으로 필요하지 않다. 유형 팁: 필요한 가정은 '부정 테스트'로 확인하고 only·no 같은 극단어 선택지는 대개 과하다. → 정답 D

items.question: Fresh apricots are 85% water by mass. A 40 kg batch is dried until water makes up 25% of the mass of the dried fruit. How much water was removed?

options.text: 24 kg
30 kg
32 kg
34 kg

items.explanation_ko: 1) 고형분은 변하지 않는다: 40 × 15% = 6 kg. 2) 말린 뒤 고형분이 75%를 차지하므로 말린 과일 질량 = 6 ÷ 0.75 = 8 kg. 3) 제거된 물 = 40 − 8 = 32 kg. 오답: A 수분 비율 차이(85% − 25% = 60%)를 처음 질량 40 kg에 곱한 값. B 말린 질량을 처음 질량의 25%(10 kg)로 착각한 값. D 물을 전부 제거했다고 본 값(34 kg). 어림 요령: 변하지 않는 양(고형분)을 기준으로 잡는다. 유형 팁: 건조·농축 문제는 변하지 않는 성분을 먼저 구한다. → 정답 C

items.stimulus:
Four people comment on solitude.

Speaker 1 (Ewan Tarr, a lighthouse keeper): People ask whether I am lonely out here. Loneliness is wanting company you cannot have. I have the sea, the lamp and my own thoughts, and most evenings I want nothing else.

Speaker 2 (Ilse Morrow, a novelist): Solitude is a room you enter by choice and leave when you please. Take away the door, and the same room becomes a cell.

Speaker 3 (Rafael Quint, a psychologist): Time alone is valuable only as a pause between conversations. The ideas we form in solitude remain unfinished until someone else has argued with them.

Speaker 4 (Hana Oyelaran, a mountaineer): On a long solo climb I talk to absent friends in my head, describing what I see. Even alone, it seems, I need an audience.
items.question: Speakers 3 and 4 would most likely agree that

options.text: even when alone, people's thinking tends to be shaped by others, whether present or imagined.
being alone is generally an unpleasant experience that most people would rather avoid whenever they can.
loneliness is the desire for company that cannot be had.
people should avoid spending long periods alone.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 화자 3: 혼자 만든 생각은 다른 사람과 논쟁해야 완성된다. 2) 화자 4: 혼자 등반하면서도 머릿속 친구들에게 이야기하며 청중이 필요하다고 느낀다. 3) 두 사람 모두 혼자 있을 때조차 생각이 타인(실제 혹은 상상 속)을 향한다고 본다. 오답: B 화자 4는 홀로 등반을 즐기며 불쾌하다고 말하지 않는다. C 화자 1의 정의다. D 화자 3의 말에서 연상될 수 있으나 '피해야 한다'는 주장은 없고 화자 4는 장시간 단독 등반을 한다. 유형 팁: 두 화자 공통 견해는 각자의 핵심 문장을 한 줄로 요약해 겹치는 부분을 찾는다. → 정답 A

items.question: How many of the unit cubes have exactly three painted faces?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 세 면이 칠해진 큐브는 직육면체의 꼭짓점에 있는 큐브다. 2) 직육면체의 꼭짓점은 크기와 상관없이 8개. 오답: A 정확히 한 면만 칠해진 큐브 수(위·아래층 가운데 각 2개). B 면의 수를 꼭짓점으로 착각한 값. C 정확히 두 면이 칠해진 큐브 수. E 칠해지지 않은 큐브 수(높이가 2라 모든 큐브가 위나 아래 면에 닿는다). 유형 팁: 칠한 면 수 문제는 꼭짓점(3면), 모서리(2면), 면 가운데(1면), 내부(0면)로 나눈다. → 정답 D

items.question: In total, how many unit-cube faces are painted?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 칠해진 면의 총수 = 블록 겉넓이(단위 정사각형 수). 2) 2 × (4 × 3 + 4 × 2 + 3 × 2) = 2 × (12 + 8 + 6) = 52. 확인: 1면 4개 + 2면 12개 × 2 + 3면 8개 × 3 = 4 + 24 + 24 = 52. 오답: A 큐브 개수(24)를 답한 값. B 4 × 3 × 2 × 2처럼 부피를 두 배 한 값. D 겉넓이 공식에서 2를 곱하지 않은 값. 유형 팁: 직육면체 겉넓이는 서로 다른 세 면을 더해 두 배 한다. → 정답 C

items.stimulus: A solid rectangular block is built from 24 identical unit cubes. The block is 4 cubes long, 3 cubes wide and 2 cubes high. The entire outside of the block, including the bottom face, is painted. The block is then taken apart into its 24 unit cubes.
items.question: How many of the unit cubes have exactly two painted faces?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 두 면이 칠해진 큐브는 꼭짓점을 제외한 모서리 위 큐브다. 2) 길이 방향 모서리 4개 × (4 − 2) = 8, 너비 방향 4개 × (3 − 2) = 4, 높이 방향 4개 × (2 − 2) = 0. 3) 합계 12. 확인: 8 + 12 + 4 = 24개로 전체와 일치. 오답: A 꼭짓점 수. C 높이 방향 모서리까지 잘못 세거나 꼭짓점을 포함한 값. D 한 면만 칠해진 큐브 수. 유형 팁: 모서리마다 (길이 − 2)개씩 세고, 전체 합이 큐브 수와 같은지 검산한다. → 정답 B

items.question: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?

options.text: If a parcel is sent by express post, it carries a red label. This parcel carries a red label. So it was sent by express post.
If a parcel is sent by express post, it carries a red label. This parcel does not carry a red label. So it was not sent by express post.
If a parcel is sent by express post, it carries a red label. This parcel was not sent by express post. So it does not carry a red label.

items.stimulus:
In several mountainous regions of the world, people have developed ways of whistling their ordinary language. On the island of La Gomera in the Canary Islands, for example, a whistled form of Spanish has long been used to send messages across deep valleys. Similar traditions have been recorded in parts of Turkey, Greece, Mexico and West Africa.

Whistled languages are not separate languages with their own vocabulary. They are a way of transmitting an existing spoken language. A whistler reduces speech to a single melodic line, keeping the features that matter most for understanding. In tonal languages, where a change of pitch can change a word's meaning, whistlers follow the pitch of the spoken words. In languages without tones, such as Spanish or Turkish, whistlers instead use changes in pitch to imitate differences between vowels and some consonants.

The advantage is distance. A loud whistle can be understood over a few kilometres, far beyond the reach of a shout, and it carries well over rough ground where walking to a neighbour might take an hour. Not surprisingly, whistled speech tends to appear where people live scattered across steep terrain and work outdoors, herding animals or tending terraced fields.

The same conditions help to explain the decline of many whistled traditions. As roads were built and telephones arrived, the practical need to whistle disappeared, and fewer children learned. Some communities have responded by teaching whistling in schools, treating it as heritage rather than as a necessary tool.

items.stimulus:
For much of the history of philosophy, a simple account of knowledge was widely accepted. To know something, it was said, three conditions must hold: you must believe it, it must be true, and you must be justified in believing it, which means you must have good reasons. A lucky guess is not knowledge, because it lacks justification; a well-supported belief that turns out to be false is not knowledge, because it lacks truth.

In the twentieth century, philosophers described cases that seemed to meet all three conditions without being knowledge. Consider an example. Priya arrives at her office and sees her colleague Tomas's distinctive green bicycle locked outside. She forms the belief that Tomas is in the building. Her belief is justified: he cycles to work every day and the bicycle is unmistakable. Her belief is also true: Tomas is at his desk. But, unknown to Priya, Tomas came by bus today, and the green bicycle belongs to a visitor who happens to own an identical one.

Most people judge that Priya does not know that Tomas is in the building. Her belief is true, but only by luck; the reason she relied on is unconnected to what actually makes it true.

Philosophers responded in several ways. Some proposed adding a fourth condition: the justification must not depend on any false belief. Priya's reasoning depended on the false belief that the bicycle was Tomas's, so the extra condition would rule out her case. Others argued that the problem lay in the idea of justification itself, and that knowledge requires a belief to be produced by a process that reliably tracks the truth. Still others concluded that no neat set of conditions will ever capture our ordinary concept of knowledge, which may work more like a family of overlapping cases than like a definition.

Afterwards, when the hall had emptied, Marguerite stayed at board eleven and set the pieces back on their squares, one by one, the way her first teacher had made her do as a girl. The boy had already gone, shaking her hand with a quick, damp grip and a 'thank you' that sounded like an apology.

She replayed the game slowly. Move nineteen was where it turned. She had seen his knight sacrifice coming, or she had seen something coming, a shape in the fog, and she had told herself it could not work. Thirty years ago she would have calculated it to the end. Today she had trusted her experience instead, and her experience had been wrong.

It was not that he was cleverer. She had beaten cleverer players. It was that he did not yet know which moves were supposed to be impossible.

The caretaker rattled his keys at the door. Marguerite lifted the white knight, turned it in her fingers and placed it on the square where the boy's knight had landed. From there, she saw now, it attacked two pieces at once. Beautiful, really. She allowed herself to admire it, the way one admires a storm that has ruined a picnic.

Then she packed the set into its wooden box, fastened the clasp and walked out into the evening, already wondering what she might learn from him when they met again at Easter.

items.stimulus:
Today a public park seems an ordinary part of city life, but in its modern form it is a fairly recent invention. Before the nineteenth century, most large green spaces in European cities belonged to royalty, the aristocracy or private societies. Some were opened to respectable visitors on certain days, but they were not created for the general public, and they were not paid for by the public.

Industrialisation changed this. As factories drew workers into cities such as Manchester and Liverpool, housing was built quickly and densely, often with little open ground. Reformers became alarmed. Many believed, wrongly as it turned out, that diseases such as cholera were spread by foul air, and they argued that open spaces would act as the 'lungs' of the city. Others hoped that parks would improve the habits of working people by offering an alternative to the tavern, or would ease tension between social classes by bringing them into the same space.

A parliamentary committee in Britain recommended in the 1830s that towns should provide open spaces for public walking, and in the following decades councils began to create them. One of the earliest, Birkenhead Park near Liverpool, opened in 1847. Its creators paid for much of it by selling plots for expensive houses around its edges, expecting that a view of the park would raise their value. Visitors from abroad came to study it, and its design influenced parks elsewhere, including in North America.

The motives behind the first public parks were therefore mixed. Concern for health sat beside a desire for social order, and civic pride beside commercial calculation. The medical theory that inspired many reformers was mistaken, yet the parks they built did benefit the health of city dwellers, if not for the reasons they gave. An idea can be defended with bad arguments and still prove to be a good idea.
